findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
findings.body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from `ctx`, which is the HTTP/API request context. That context is normally canceled as soon as the handler returns the successful unified-storage response, so the asynchronously scheduled legacy `Create` can be canceled before or during execution. The same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163). This makes the intended legacy safety copy unreliable in normal request handling. Derive the background replication context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (while retaining relevant values) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Independent replication goroutines can apply writes to legacy out of order
findings.body: Each successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a client can create an object and immediately update or delete it; the legacy update/delete goroutine may run before the legacy create goroutine, causing the update/delete to fail and then leaving the subsequently created legacy object stale. The same issue applies to successive updates. Since errors are ignored, this can permanently leave legacy storage inconsistent even though all unified writes succeeded. Replication needs ordered processing (at least per object/collection) or a mechanism to reconcile/retry failed operations.

findings.title: Update recomputes the request's updated object separately for legacy storage
findings.body: After `Storage.Update` has consumed `objInfo`, the async legacy update receives the original `objInfo` again rather than a wrapper around the object produced by unified storage. `UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject` can be stateful or depend on the old object (notably patch/apply semantics, generated fields, and managed fields), so it is now evaluated twice against potentially different old objects. Consequently unified and legacy can receive different updates, or the second evaluation can fail. The previous implementation computed the updated object once and passed an `updateWrapper` containing that result to both stores; preserve that single computed result for the legacy replication.

findings.title: Several mode-3 metrics are recorded against the wrong backend or label
findings.body: A unified-storage Create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` here, and the equivalent Update failure does the same at line 129, so storage failures are attributed to legacy. Delete success at line 106 uses `name` as the kind label rather than `options.Kind`, creating unbounded/high-cardinality per-object metric labels. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy replication duration/errors are reported as storage metrics. These errors make the new mode's operational telemetry misleading and can create excessive metric cardinality.
